title: Relational databases, ACID and transactions

kcs.statement: A relational database stores data as rows in tables with a fixed schema and links tables through foreign keys, which SQL joins follow at query time.

ACID means atomicity (all of a transaction's writes commit or none do), consistency (constraints hold after every commit), isolation (concurrent transactions do not see each other's partial work) and durability (committed data survives a crash).
Multi-row changes that must succeed together, such as debiting one account and crediting another, belong in one transaction so a crash midway leaves neither change applied.

problem_ideas: A money transfer debits A, then the server crashes before crediting B: which ACID letter prevents the lost money?
Two users book the last seat at the same moment: which property decides that only one succeeds?
Classify each of five bugs (half-written order, negative stock, phantom read, lost commit after power cut) under the ACID letter that would prevent it
Given an e-commerce schema with users, orders and order_items, write the foreign keys and the join that lists a user's orders
Decide which of six operations (like a post, place an order, update a profile photo URL, transfer credits) truly need a multi-row transaction
Explain to an interviewer why 'consistency' in ACID is about constraints, not about replicas agreeing
